metadata.greeting_note: Plain English hello, narrator is Anjana; no channel handle or brand chip on this build.

beats.narration_text: Everyone says a language model turns words into numbers. Nobody says which numbers, or where they come from, or why they end up where they do. I'm Anjana — let's open the table.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself
runningText 'opening the table…'
output lines resolve, already answered

props.command: A model converts every token into a vector before it does anything else. Where do those numbers come from, and what do the distances between them actually mean?
output: a lookup table, learned not programmed
similar meanings land near each other

beats.narration_text: Hello, Anjana here. A large language model does not read words. It reads numbers. Every token that enters the model gets converted into a long list of numbers called a vector. That vector is the embedding. And what it stores is more interesting than you think.

show.event: the word 'revenue' fades in on the left with a soft glow
a flowing line carries it to the right
the word dissolves into particles that reform as a column of signed decimals
the label '768 dimensions' fades in beside the column
the numbers pulse gently in embedding blue

props.sparkLine: A word becomes a list of numbers.

beats.narration_text: Before the model does anything else, it checks a table. Every token in its vocabulary has a row in this table. Each row is a vector, randomly initialized at first, then shaped during training. The model learns what numbers to assign to each token by reading billions of sentences. No one programs these values. They emerge.

show.event: the embedding matrix fades in — seven labelled rows, columns dim 1 … dim 768
the 'revenue' row lights blue
the highlighted row slides out of the matrix, becoming the standalone vector
the training bar appears below: noise on the left, structure on the right
the sweep runs left to right, leaving structured values behind it

beats.narration_text: Here is what makes embeddings powerful. Words with similar meanings end up near each other. Revenue growth and sales increase land in the same neighborhood. Write-down and impairment cluster together somewhere else. The distance between two vectors tells you how related two concepts are. The model learned this structure entirely from context.

show.event: an empty 2D projection of embedding space
green dots arrive one by one in the upper right with labels
a dashed green ring closes around them
red dots fill the lower left, then their own dashed ring
a short gold measure between 'growth' and 'raised' — similar
a long gold measure between 'growth' and 'decline' — distant

beats.narration_text: But static embeddings are just the start. In a large language model, the same token gets a different vector depending on context. The word bank next to river produces one embedding. Bank next to earnings produces a completely different one. That is what the transformer layers do. They take the initial embedding and reshape it based on every other token in the sequence. By the final layer, the vector no longer represents just a word. It represents that word's meaning in this specific sentence.

show.event: top sentence appears: the · river · bank · was · steep; 'bank' rings blue
its arrow flows through three purple transformer blocks
a dot drifts out and lands in the green nature cluster
bottom sentence appears: the · bank · reported · strong · earnings; 'bank' rings gold
its arrow flows through its own transformer blocks
a second dot lands in the orange finance cluster
between the two paths: 'same token, different vectors'

beats.narration_text: Embeddings are not just numbers. They are learned geometry. Every relationship the model understands lives in the distances and directions between these vectors.

show.event: the scatter from B03 returns, fuller
a grey neutral cluster fills the centre; boundaries glow in their own colors
a slow parallax drift gives the space depth
the title settles underneath: What Embeddings Actually Store

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The numbers are not written by anyone. They start random and get shaped by training. Position carries meaning — similar words end up as near neighbours because they showed up in similar company. And in a transformer, the vector you start with is not the vector you end with. The layers rewrite it until it means this word, in this sentence.

show.event: 0.5s lead pause, then ClaudeVerdictArtifact card builds in
line 1: the learned-table line settles in
line 2: distance encodes relatedness
line 3: the layers rewrite the initial embedding
line 4: a word in a sentence, not a word

artifactLines: Every token has a row in a learned table; the values start random and are shaped by training.
Distance encodes relatedness — the structure comes from context, not from a dictionary.
Transformer layers rewrite the initial embedding using the rest of the sequence.
By the final layer the vector represents a word in a sentence, not a word.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take any vocabulary you work in — ticker symbols, product codes, diagnosis codes, tags — and ask what its geometry would look like. Which of your items would be near neighbours, what would have to be true for that to happen, and what a distance between two of them would actually mean.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Your turn.'; prompt types itself
runningText 'mapping your vocabulary…'

props.command: I work with a fixed vocabulary of items — codes, tags, symbols, categories. Can you help me: one, sketch what an embedding space over my vocabulary would cluster into, and say which clusters are real structure versus wishful thinking; two, name what data would have to exist for those clusters to be learnable at all; and three, tell me honestly whether distance between two of my items would mean anything useful, or whether I'd be reading shapes in noise?

subline fades in: 'learned geometry · not a dictionary'
